newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Yeltsin talks tough on NATO, phones Western leaders.
newsitem.headline: Yeltsin talks tough on NATO, phones Western leaders.

text.p: Russian President Boris Yeltsin stepped up his personal telephone diplomacy with NATO leaders on Tuesday but told his top negotiator to take a tough line in talks with the Western defence alliance on its plans for enlargement.

The Kremlin said Yeltsin discussed security matters with West German Chancellor Helmut Kohl and new British Prime Minister Tony Blair, following a conversation with French President Jacques Chirac on Monday.

Itar-Tass news agency said Yeltsin had instructed Foreign Minister Yevgeny Primakov to take a firm line in defending Russia's interests at Tuesday's meeting in Moscow with NATO Secretary General Javier Solana.

"The president confirmed the foreign minister's mandate for the talks and noted the need to continue the firm Russian line, based on defending the country's interests especially on... military questions," Tass said, quoting presidential press secretary Sergei Yastrzhembsky.
Solana was due in Moscow on Tuesday evening for the talks which Primakov says will show whether Russia and NATO can sign an agreement on a new relationship after years of mistrust.

Some Kremlin sources say Russia has already decided to sign the deal in Paris on May 27 but will keep up the uncertainty and anti-NATO rhetoric until the last minute to appease domestic opponents who fear Yeltsin is selling out national interests.
The Kremlin gave few details of Yeltsin's conversations with Kohl and Blair, and did not say if they would have any impact on the outcome of Primakov's talks with Solana.
A group of influentual Russian foreign policy experts warned the Kremlin against signing a quick but imperfect deal with NATO, saying it might be wiser to prolong talks.

"Although steps have been taken in the right direction in the last few months, and the Russian president and foreign minister have obtained movement from the Western side, too much remains in the zone of uncertainty," said the declaration, published by the newspaper Nezavisimaya Gazeta.
The declaration was issued by the Advisory Council on Foreign and Defence Policy, which broadly backs Yeltsin but has no direct influence on policy.
Primakov said Russia still hoped Tuesday's talks with Solana would be the last before May 27.
"We would like it to be so, but not everything depends on us. Let us wait and see what Mr Solana brings," he told a news conference with visiting Swiss Foreign Minister Flavio Cotti.
The Russia-NATO deal is intended to overcome Moscow's strong objections to the North Atlantic Treaty Organisation's plans to expand to take in new members from the former Soviet bloc.
Solana, who last met Primakov in Luxembourg last week, was expected to keep a low public profile when he arrived in Moscow at around 6 p.m. (1400 GMT) and not to meet reporters.
Yeltsin does not plan to meet Solana but may telephone him during his stay in Moscow, Yastrzhembsky said.

The main disagreements over a deal defining a new partnership between the former Cold War foes include Moscow's demands for written guarantees that the alliance will not move its military might into new member states.
Russia is also demanding progress over amending a 1990 treaty governing conventional arms in Europe and a say in decision-making on security issues.
Invitations to new NATO members are due to go out at an alliance summit in Madrid in July.
Poland, Hungary and the Czech Republic are thought be the leading contenders to join NATO, but Romania and Slovenia also hope to be in the first wave of new members.
